title: What is financial leverage?
subtitle: Leverage amplifies both gains and losses. It's a genuine double-edged sword.
openingQuestion: You have 100 million of your own capital. You buy 100 million of stock; it rises 20%, earning 20 million (20% on capital). Or you borrow an extra 300 million to buy 400 million; it rises 20%, earning 80 million before loan interest. What is the ROE when using leverage?
openingOptions: It can't be calculated without knowing the loan's interest rate
80%, since the 80 million gain sits on 100 million of own capital
Roughly 50-60% after paying loan interest, depending on the rate
explanation: Leverage means investing on a larger base than your own capital by using borrowed money. With 100 million of own capital plus 300 million borrowed, a 20% rise in the asset produces an 80-million gain; after paying loan interest, roughly 56 million is left, meaning a 56% return on your own capital rather than 20%. But the mechanism runs exactly the same way in reverse: a 20% drop in the asset loses 80 million on 100 million of capital, and you still owe the interest on top. Leverage doesn't create profit - it only multiplies whatever the outcome turns out to be.

diagram.label: Invest on a larger total base
Loan interest is a fixed cost paid first
Whatever remains lands entirely on your own capital: gains and losses both amplified

realWorldExample.description: In 2008, Lehman Brothers ran a leverage ratio of 30:1 (every 1 dollar of capital controlled 30 dollars of assets). When its assets lost just 3.3% of their value, its entire capital was wiped out. This was the cause of its collapse.

quiz.question: What does financial leverage amplify?
options: It amplifies revenue but leaves the profit margin unchanged
It amplifies gains but caps losses at the amount of own capital
It only amplifies gains when the market is rising
It amplifies both gains and losses relative to own capital
quiz.explanation: Leverage is a double-edged sword. If the investment does well, ROE rises many times over. If it does badly, the loss is amplified just as much, and can exceed the own capital put in if not managed.

quiz.question: What does a leverage ratio of 4:1 mean?
options: 1 dong of own capital controls 4 dong of assets
Every 4 dong of profit is needed to pay 1 dong of loan interest
You've borrowed 4 times your annual income
The asset is expected to grow 4 times over within a year
quiz.explanation: Leverage 4:1 = total assets of 400 million, own capital of 100 million, debt of 300 million. Every 1% move in total assets produces a 4% move in own capital.

quiz.question: Scenario: You have 200 million of own capital. Option A: invest without leverage, expecting a 15% a year return. Option B: borrow an extra 600 million (total 800 million) at 8% a year, expecting a 15% a year return on the total assets. If the market rises 15%, what is the ROE of each option? What if the market falls 10%?
options: A: 15%/-10%; B: 15%/-10% (ignoring leverage)
A: 15%/-10%; B: 36%/-64% (correct in both directions)
A: 15%/-10%; B: 27%/-34% (forgetting the loan interest)
A: 15%/-10%; B: 60%/-40% (simply multiplying by 4)
quiz.explanation: On a 15% rise: A = 15%. B: profit = 800×15% − 600×8% = 120 − 48 = 72 million. ROE = 72/200 = 36%. On a 10% fall: A = -10%. B: loss = 800×(-10%) − 600×8% = -80 − 48 = -128 million. ROE = -128/200 = -64%. Leverage amplifies both the wins and the losses.

quiz.question: Scenario: You have 200 million of own capital and borrow an extra 600 million to invest. What is the leverage ratio?
options: 1:3 (= 200 ÷ 600, the ratio inverted)
3:1 (= 600 borrowed ÷ 200 capital, leaving out own capital from the total)
4:1 (= 800 million total assets ÷ 200 million capital)
8:1 (= 800 ÷ 100, dividing by the wrong denominator)
quiz.explanation: The leverage ratio takes total assets divided by own capital: (200 + 600) ÷ 200 = 4. This figure shows how many dong of assets each dong of your capital is controlling, and it is exactly the multiplier applied to both gains and losses.

quiz.question: Scenario: Leverage of 4:1 on 200 million of own capital. The asset's value falls 25%. How much of your own capital is left?
options: Unchanged, because the loss falls on the lender
Down 25%, leaving 150 million, matching the asset's fall
Down 6.25% (= 25% ÷ 4), leaving 187 million
Wiped out entirely (= 800 × 25% = 200, exactly equal to your capital)
quiz.explanation: The loss is calculated on the entire asset, not on your capital alone: 800 × 25% = 200 million, exactly equal to your own capital. A 4:1 leverage ratio means the asset only needs to fall 25% to wipe your capital out completely - which is why high leverage and heavy volatility don't mix.

keyTakeaways: Leverage amplifies both gains and losses relative to own capital
Leverage ratio: total assets / own capital
High leverage plus market volatility is a recipe for insolvency

practicePrompt.question: You're considering borrowing an extra 300 million to buy stocks, raising your total invested capital from 100 million to 400 million. The market has a 50% chance of rising 20% and a 50% chance of falling 20% over the next year. How would this decision to borrow and invest affect you?
options: It amplifies both directions: if the market rises you gain far more than your own capital's worth, but if it falls you could lose most or all of your own capital
It only amplifies gains when you win, while a loss would only cost you the borrowed amount, not your own capital
It wouldn't affect you much, since loan interest is usually far smaller than a stock's short-term price swings
It reduces risk, because holding a larger-valued position makes percentage moves relatively smaller
practicePrompt.explanation: Leverage amplifies both gains and losses relative to own capital - this is simply the mathematics of borrowing to invest, regardless of whether you personally 'feel' the risk or not.

summary.keyIdea: Leverage amplifies both gains and losses relative to own capital
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: Leverage ratio: total assets / own capital

application.title: Calculate ROE with and without leverage yourself
application.message: Take a hypothetical amount of own capital (say, 100 million), assume you borrow 3 times that at 8% interest, then calculate ROE under two scenarios - a 20% gain and a 20% loss - to see how leverage amplifies each.
application.secondary: The loss figure in the bad scenario is usually more startling than expected.

sections.text: You have 100 million of own capital. Buy 100 million of stock and it rises 20% - a 20-million gain. Or borrow an extra 300 million, buy 400 million, and it rises 20% - an 80-million gain before loan interest. Leverage turns 100 million of capital into 400 million of buying power - but this is a genuine double-edged sword.

Financial leverage is using borrowed capital to expand the scale of an investment far beyond your own capital, in order to amplify the return on each dong invested. If the invested asset rises in price, leverage multiplies the profit many times over compared with using only your own capital.
A double-edged sword: amplified in both directions

In the example: an 80-million gain, minus loan interest of 8%×300 million = 24 million, leaves 56 million of net profit on 100 million of own capital → ROE = 56%, far higher than the 20% without leverage. But if the stock FELL 20% instead of rising: you lose 80 million on a 400-million asset, plus 24 million of loan interest still owed - a total loss of 104 million, EXCEEDING the original 100 million of own capital. This is the core risk of leverage: it amplifies gains and losses at exactly the same rate.

items: Leverage amplifies both gains and losses relative to own capital, favouring neither direction
Leverage ratio = total assets / own capital - the higher it is, the greater the amplification
High leverage combined with sharp market volatility can wipe out capital entirely, or even leave debt exceeding assets

sections.label: A rule for using leverage safely
sections.text: Only use leverage once you clearly understand and can accept the worst-case scenario, not just the favourable one. Leverage suits an experienced investor with a solid financial safety margin, not a tool for someone just starting out.

lines: Leverage is neither good nor bad in itself - it is only an amplifying tool. Amplifying a sound decision produces an excellent result; amplifying a poor one leads to disaster much faster.
